lines.text: A post comes down onto a sill. A tongue on its end slides into a hole, and a square pin is driven across, pulling the two tight together.

lines.text: There are many named kinds. A doubled tenon, the jūhozo, for example, goes at the top of a post where a wall plate and a beam stack up. This episode looks at the joint where a post meets a sill.

lines.text: The Flat 35 house specification gives two everyday options there. A short tenon, with a metal plate or bracket to hold it down. Or a long tenon, pinned with a komisen.

lines.text: How big is a short tenon? Japan's standard test for joint hardware uses one on a hundred-and-five millimeter post: thirty thick, eighty-five wide, fifty deep.

lines.text: Notice what the specification's rating table says: a short tenon on its own is rated at zero. The hardware does the holding.

lines.text: The long tenon goes most of the way through the sill. A hardwood pin, the komisen, is driven sideways through sill and tenon together. Where the tenon passes right through and sticks out, it can be pinned through that projecting part instead: a hanasen.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: The long tenon goes most of the way through the sill. A hardwood pin, the koh-mee-sen, is driven sideways through sill and tenon together. Where the tenon passes right through and sticks out, it can be pinned through that projecting part instead: a hah-nah-sen.

lines.text: The holes are made so the pin draws the two members together: the hole in the tenon sits slightly toward the shoulder. Driving the pin pulls the post down tight onto the sill.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: The public-works specification asks for square holes and square pins; round pins are now used more and more. In a bearing wall, the loan specification rates a pinned long tenon the same as a metal corner bracket.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 125 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, short crisp vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Cutting the tenon: rip down the cheeks, then crosscut the shoulder, sawing on the waste side of the line. The public-works specification warns: don't saw the shoulder cut too deep.

lines.text: In the skills-test manual's practice piece, the tenon's thickness is cut a little loose and its width a little tight, as we saw in Episode 4.

lines.text: Chopping the mortise: use a mortise chisel a little narrower than the hole. Start a few millimeters inside the lines, rough it out, then pare back to the lines and check the depth.

lines.text: The manual adds: strike lightly when the edge runs along the grain, and harder when it cuts across it.

lines.text: Fit it in small steps. The width should go in with light taps over a block of wood; the thickness, by hand. The finished joint should be snug: driven in, and fully seated.
